title: Osasuna Goalkeeper Gets Bizarre Red Card After Handling Ball Way Outside the Box
excerpt: Sergio Herrera's attempt to head the ball outside his penalty area went wrong when his hand made contact, leaving Osasuna down to ten men in a La Liga clash against Levante.
body:
• Osasuna goalkeeper Sergio Herrera was sent off after attempting to head the ball outside the penalty area but accidentally touching it with his left hand during a La Liga match against Levante.
  • The referee showed an immediate red card for denying a goal-scoring opportunity, leaving Osasuna to play the second half with ten men.
  • Levante went on to win the match 3-2 as Osasuna could not recover from the numerical disadvantage.

Goalkeepers handle the ball hundreds of times per match. It is, quite literally, their job. But step a few yards beyond the white line marking the penalty area, and those same hands become a liability — as Osasuna's Sergio Herrera discovered in spectacularly viral fashion.

During a La Liga match against Levante in May, Herrera rushed out of his penalty box to deal with a through ball. Recognizing he was outside his area, the Spanish goalkeeper tried to play the ball with his head — a manoeuvre that requires a certain amount of poise under pressure. Poise, unfortunately, was in short supply.

The Moment That Broke Social Media

In the confusion of the split-second decision, Herrera's left hand made clear contact with the ball. The Levante bench erupted instantly, players jumping to their feet and pointing at the goalkeeper. The referee had no hesitation: straight red card.

Video replays confirmed what everyone at the stadium already knew. Herrera's intention to head the ball was evident, but the execution was fatally flawed. The ball deflected off his hand before touching his head, constituting deliberate handball outside the penalty area. Under the Laws of the Game, a goalkeeper outside the box is treated like any outfield player — and a handball that denies an obvious goal-scoring opportunity (DOGSO) is a sending-off offence.

The clip quickly went viral across social media, racking up millions of views and earning a place in the growing canon of goalkeeper blunders. OneFootball described it as "the most viral sending-off of the matchday."

What the Rules Say

The International Football Association Board (IFAB), which governs the Laws of the Game, is clear on the matter. A goalkeeper has the same restrictions on handling the ball as any other player outside the penalty area. Whether the offence merits a yellow or red card depends on the impact on the attacking team.

If the handball denies an obvious goal-scoring opportunity — as the referee judged in Herrera's case — a red card is mandatory. The distinction matters: it is not the handball itself that draws the send-off, but the effect of preventing a likely goal.

The rule has produced memorable moments across world football. Manchester City's Claudio Bravo was sent off for a similar offence against Barcelona in the Champions League in 2016 after instinctively blocking Luis Suárez's shot outside the box. More recently, Juventus goalkeeper Michele Di Gregorio received a straight red against RB Leipzig in the 2024-25 Champions League after touching the ball with his hand while rushing out of his area.

The Fallout for Osasuna

Reduced to ten men for the entire second half, Osasuna could not hold on. Levante capitalized on the numerical advantage to win 3-2 in a match that might otherwise have been an unremarkable mid-table affair. For Herrera, a veteran of La Liga, the incident was a painful reminder that the margin between an impressive sweeper-keeper clearance and a career-defining embarrassment is measured in centimetres.

A Growing Catalogue of Keeper Calamities

Herrera joins a long and inglorious list of goalkeepers undone by the boundary line. The 2026 FIFA World Cup has already added to the genre, with record numbers of red cards — thirteen in total — and new rules on confrontational behaviour testing the limits of on-field discipline. The trend toward sweeper-keeper play, popularized by the likes of Manuel Neuer and Ederson, has pushed goalkeepers further from their line than ever, increasing the risk of exactly the kind of error Herrera committed.

For fans, these moments are pure entertainment — the kind of clip that defines a matchday and outlives any tactical analysis. For goalkeepers, they are a reminder: outside the box, your hands are just another pair of liabilities.
